international_coffee_day.label: International Coffee Day
international_coffee_day.intro: A worldwide toast to the bean that gets most of the planet out of bed. Filter, espresso or cold brew – the point is to enjoy the cup and spare a thought for the people who grow it.
funFacts: The International Coffee Organization launched the shared date in Milan in 2015; several countries had been holding their own coffee day before that.
Finland drinks more coffee per head than any other country, well over ten kilograms of roasted beans per person a year.
A coffee cherry normally holds two flat-sided seeds; when only one round seed forms, it is called a peaberry.

name_your_car_day.label: National Name Your Car Day
name_your_car_day.intro: Plenty of people talk to their car anyway, so today it officially gets a name. A silly little ritual that turns a lump of metal into a member of the household.
funFacts: Cars have collected nicknames since the beginning: Ford's Model T was known to everyone as the Tin Lizzie.
Herbie, the Volkswagen Beetle of the Disney films, races with the number 53, borrowed from baseball pitcher Don Drysdale.
The Beetle itself is named after insects around the world: Käfer in Germany, coccinelle (ladybird) in France, maggiolino (may bug) in Italy.

mean_girls_day.label: Mean Girls Day
mean_girls_day.intro: One line of film dialogue turned 3 October into a fan holiday. Every year the internet quotes it, wears pink and rewatches the whole comedy.
funFacts: The date comes from a single scene: Aaron turns around, asks Cady what day it is, and she answers that it is October 3rd.
Tina Fey wrote the screenplay after reading Rosalind Wiseman's non-fiction book about teenage cliques, Queen Bees and Wannabes.
Fans often wear pink on the day, a nod to the film's rule that the clique dresses in pink on Wednesdays.

taco_day.label: National Taco Day
taco_day.intro: A folded tortilla, a filling, a squeeze of lime – and an endless argument about the right one. Today every version counts, from street-stall al pastor to the crunchy shell at home.
funFacts: In 19th-century Mexican silver mines a taco was a paper-wrapped charge of gunpowder, which is the likeliest source of the food's name.
Tacos al pastor grew out of the spit-roasted meat that Lebanese immigrants brought to Mexico in the early 20th century.
The pre-formed crunchy shell is a US invention that spread with fast-food chains from the 1950s onwards.

james_bond_day.label: Global James Bond Day
james_bond_day.intro: Shaken, not stirred: the day marks the anniversary of the very first Bond film and belongs to everyone who enjoys gadgets, chase scenes and a good title song.
funFacts: The first Global James Bond Day was held on 5 October 2012, fifty years to the day after Dr. No premiered in London.
Ian Fleming borrowed the name from the American ornithologist James Bond, author of the field guide Birds of the West Indies.
Six actors have played 007 in the official film series so far, from Sean Connery to Daniel Craig.

mad_hatter_day.label: Mad Hatter Day
mad_hatter_day.intro: A day for cheerful nonsense, borrowed from Lewis Carroll's tea party. The invitation is simple: be a little more absurd than usual and put the kettle on.
funFacts: The date comes from the card in the Hatter's hatband in John Tenniel's 1865 illustrations: 10/6, a price of ten shillings and sixpence.
Computer staff in Boulder, Colorado declared the day in 1986 as an antidote to overly serious workdays.
The saying mad as a hatter is older than the book: hat makers worked with mercury compounds, which damaged the nervous system.

frappe_day.label: National Frappe Day
frappe_day.intro: Instant coffee, sugar and water shaken into a thick foam, then poured over ice: the frappe is Greece's gift to hot afternoons, and it was invented completely by accident.
funFacts: The drink was improvised at the 1957 Thessaloniki trade fair, when a Nestle representative had no hot water for his coffee.
In Greece you order it sketos, metrios or glykos, meaning without sugar, with some, or sweet.
The foam only works with instant coffee: its soluble powder whips up in a way that freshly brewed coffee cannot.

world_octopus_day.label: World Octopus Day
world_octopus_day.intro: A day for the most alien-looking clever animal in the ocean. Eight arms, an escape-artist reputation and a talent for opening jars make the octopus hard not to admire.
funFacts: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood, because it carries oxygen with copper-based haemocyanin instead of iron.
About two thirds of its neurons sit in the arms, which can feel and taste on their own.
It changes colour and texture within a fraction of a second, even though its eyes are almost certainly colour-blind.

beer_and_pizza_day.label: International Beer and Pizza Day
beer_and_pizza_day.intro: The most reliable pairing in the world gets its own date. A hot slice, a cold glass, no cutlery required – ideally shared with other people.
funFacts: Legend has it the Margherita's basil, mozzarella and tomato were chosen for Queen Margherita's visit to Naples in 1889.
The craft of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo has been on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage since 2017.
The Bavarian purity law of 1516 named only barley, hops and water; yeast was still unknown as an ingredient.

cake_decorating_day.label: National Cake Decorating Day
cake_decorating_day.intro: Today the icing matters more than the sponge. Piping bag, spatula and a steady hand turn an ordinary cake into something people photograph before they eat it.
funFacts: The piping bag is usually credited to the French chef Antonin Careme, who built showpiece confections in the early 19th century.
Royal icing, the hard white kind, is said to owe its name to Queen Victoria's wedding cake of 1840.
Rolled fondant is laid over a cake in one sheet, which is why the surface can look as smooth as porcelain.

dulce_de_leche_day.label: World Dulce de Leche Day
dulce_de_leche_day.intro: Milk and sugar, stirred until they turn deep brown and spreadable. South America's favourite sweet goes on toast, into pastries and, most often, straight onto a spoon.
funFacts: The Argentinian dulce de leche trade association has promoted 11 October as its day since 1998.
The colour and flavour come from slow caramelisation and browning reactions between milk sugar and milk protein.
A popular legend puts its invention in 1829, when a maid supposedly forgot a pot of sweetened milk on the stove.

gumbo_day.label: National Gumbo Day
gumbo_day.intro: Louisiana in a bowl: a thick stew of roux, stock and whatever the region offers, served over rice. Every family cooks it slightly differently and defends its version.
funFacts: Everything starts with the roux, flour cooked in fat and stirred until it goes from blond to dark chocolate brown.
The name most likely comes from a West African word for okra, one of the classic thickeners.
Louisiana declared gumbo its official state cuisine in 2004.

treat_yo_self_day.label: Treat Yo' Self Day
treat_yo_self_day.intro: A sitcom invented it and fans kept it: one day a year for guilt-free indulgence, whether that means new shoes, a long bath or an absurdly large dessert.
funFacts: The phrase comes from the Parks and Recreation episode Pawnee Rangers, first broadcast on 13 October 2011.
In the show Tom and Donna spend the day on clothes, fragrances, massages, mimosas and fine leather goods.
Their friend Ben joins in and blows his budget on a full Batman costume, which he then refuses to take off.

dessert_day.label: National Dessert Day
dessert_day.intro: The course everyone claims to have no room for and then finishes anyway. Cake, pudding, ice cream or fruit – today the sweet ending is the main event.
funFacts: The word dessert comes from the French desservir, to clear the table: it was what arrived after everything else was taken away.
Tiramisu is surprisingly young; the recipe is traced to restaurants around Treviso in the 1960s and 70s.
A baked Alaska survives the oven because whipped egg white is full of air and insulates the ice cream underneath.

pug_day.label: National Pug Day
pug_day.intro: Snorting, wrinkled and thoroughly convinced of its own charm: the pug gets a day of its own. A breed built entirely for company rather than work.
funFacts: Pugs come from China, where they were bred centuries ago as lapdogs for the imperial court.
A group of pugs is traditionally called a grumble.
In the Netherlands the pug became a symbol of the House of Orange after one is said to have woken William the Silent in time.

world_bread_day.label: World Bread Day
world_bread_day.intro: Flour, water, salt and time. Bread is the most ordinary food there is and one of the most varied – today bakers and home bakers celebrate exactly that.
funFacts: Bakers' associations started the day in 2006, deliberately placing it alongside World Food Day on 16 October.
German bread culture, with more than 3,000 registered varieties, is listed as national intangible cultural heritage.
Sourdough rises without added yeast: wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria in the starter do the work.

mulligan_day.label: Mulligan Day
mulligan_day.intro: In golf a mulligan is a shot you simply take again, unpunished. The day borrows that idea for everything else: one friendly do-over, no questions asked.
funFacts: The most repeated origin story credits the Canadian golfer David Mulligan, who re-teed a bad drive in Montreal in the 1920s.
The official rules of golf do not recognise the mulligan at all; it exists only in friendly rounds.
Charity tournaments often sell mulligans in advance, which turns a bad shot into a donation.

necktie_day.label: International Necktie Day
necktie_day.intro: Croatia celebrates the accessory it gave the world. The cravat travelled from a soldier's neck cloth to the boardroom – and the knot is still a small daily ritual.
funFacts: The word cravat goes back to Croatian soldiers in 17th-century France, whose knotted neck cloths became a court fashion.
In 2003 a huge red cravat was tied around the Roman amphitheatre in Pula to mark the day.
The modern tie owes its shape to Jesse Langsdorf, who patented cutting the fabric on the bias in 1924.

gin_and_tonic_day.label: International Gin and Tonic Day
gin_and_tonic_day.intro: Two ingredients, endless variations: gin, tonic, ice and something citrus. A drink that started out as medicine and became the easiest cocktail in the world.
funFacts: British troops in India mixed bitter quinine tonic with gin, sugar and lime to make their malaria prophylaxis drinkable.
The quinine in tonic water fluoresces under ultraviolet light, which makes the glass glow pale blue.
London Dry Gin is a production method, not a place of origin: it can legally be distilled anywhere in the world.

sloth_day.label: International Sloth Day
sloth_day.intro: The slowest mammal in the tree tops gets its own day. Sloths do everything at half speed and still manage to be excellent swimmers – a good argument for taking your time.
funFacts: The Colombian wildlife foundation AIUNAU started the day in 2010 after an international sloth meeting in Medellin.
Sloth fur grows from the belly towards the back, so rain runs off while the animal hangs upside down.
Green algae grow in that fur as camouflage, and specialised sloth moths live in it too.

apple_day.label: Apple Day
apple_day.intro: A British autumn celebration of apples and the orchards they come from, with tastings, pressing and forgotten varieties on the table.
funFacts: The charity Common Ground held the first Apple Day on 21 October 1990 in London's Covent Garden.
The National Fruit Collection in Kent keeps more than 2,000 apple varieties growing side by side.
Apple pips never grow true to the parent tree, so every orchard variety is propagated by grafting.

wombat_day.label: Wombat Day
wombat_day.intro: Australia's sturdy burrowing marsupial gets a day of appreciation. Short legs, powerful claws and an unbothered attitude have earned the wombat a lot of fans.
funFacts: Wombats are the only animals known to produce cube-shaped droppings, which stay put on rocks instead of rolling away.
Their pouch opens backwards, so digging does not fill it with soil while a joey is inside.
The rear end is reinforced with tough cartilage, and wombats use it to block the entrance of their burrow.

mole_day.label: Mole Day
mole_day.intro: Chemistry's own party: from 6:02 in the morning to 6:02 in the evening on 10/23, classrooms celebrate the unit that makes counting atoms possible.
funFacts: The date and time spell out Avogadro's number, 6.02 times ten to the twenty-third.
Since the 2019 redefinition of the SI units, one mole contains exactly 6.02214076 times ten to the twenty-third particles.
The idea appeared in a chemistry teachers' journal in the 1980s; the National Mole Day Foundation followed in 1991.

bologna_day.label: National Bologna Day
bologna_day.intro: The pale pink slice between two pieces of bread: bologna is unglamorous lunchbox food with an Italian ancestor and a lot of nostalgia attached.
funFacts: The sausage takes its name from Bologna's mortadella, but leaves out the cubes of fat and the pistachios.
Mortadella di Bologna has carried EU protected geographical indication status since 1998.
In the United States a 1970s advertising jingle that spelled out the name made bologna a household word.

world_pasta_day.label: World Pasta Day
world_pasta_day.intro: Durum wheat, water, boiling salted water: pasta is the cheapest reliable happiness there is. The day was invented by pasta makers and adopted by everyone else.
funFacts: The date was proclaimed at the first World Pasta Congress in Rome on 25 October 1995.
Italy counts hundreds of shapes, and the same shape often carries a different name from region to region.
Italian law requires dried pasta to be made from durum wheat semolina, which is what keeps it firm when cooked.

pumpkin_day.label: National Pumpkin Day
pumpkin_day.intro: Soup, pie, lantern or doorstep decoration: October belongs to the pumpkin. Today it is celebrated as a vegetable rather than a face with a candle in it.
funFacts: Botanically a pumpkin is a berry, and it belongs to the same family as cucumbers and melons.
Competition growers have pushed the world record for a single pumpkin past 1,200 kilograms.
Before pumpkins were available, Irish lanterns were carved from turnips and beets.

black_cat_day.label: National Black Cat Day
black_cat_day.intro: A day for the cats that get overlooked. Black cats wait longest in shelters and photograph badly – and are otherwise exactly like every other cat.
funFacts: The British charity Cats Protection started the day in 2011 because black cats were being adopted more slowly than others.
In Britain and Japan a black cat crossing your path is considered lucky, while much of continental Europe reads it the other way round.
Most black cats carry a hidden tabby pattern that becomes visible in bright sunlight.

international_animation_day.label: International Animation Day
international_animation_day.intro: Drawn, modelled or rendered: today celebrates the art of making still images move, and the enormous patience it takes to do it well.
funFacts: The date marks 28 October 1892, when Emile Reynaud showed his Theatre Optique to a paying audience in Paris.
The international animation association ASIFA has organised screenings on the day since 2002.
Film normally runs at 24 frames a second; hand-drawn animation often uses one drawing for two or three frames.

internet_day.label: International Internet Day
internet_day.intro: The day the network first spoke. It celebrates the very first message sent between two distant computers – which promptly crashed halfway through.
funFacts: On 29 October 1969 UCLA sent the word login to Stanford; the system failed after the letters L and O.
The ARPANET started with four nodes: UCLA, the Stanford Research Institute, UC Santa Barbara and the University of Utah.
The smiley made of a colon and a bracket was proposed by computer scientist Scott Fahlman in 1982.

candy_corn_day.label: National Candy Corn Day
candy_corn_day.intro: Three stripes of sugar in the shape of a kernel of corn: America's most divisive sweet. People either eat a whole bag or refuse to touch it.
funFacts: Candy corn was created in the 1880s by George Renninger at the Wunderlee Candy Company in Philadelphia.
It was originally marketed to farmers as chicken feed and sold all year, not just in autumn.
The white, orange and yellow layers were once poured into moulds by hand, one colour after another.

magic_day.label: National Magic Day
magic_day.intro: Cards, coins and a little misdirection: magicians mark this date in memory of Harry Houdini, who died on 31 October 1926.
funFacts: Houdini led the Society of American Magicians for nine years, and the society has kept the date ever since.
His best known escapes involved handcuffs, straitjackets and the water-filled Chinese Water Torture Cell.
The cups and balls routine is one of the oldest recorded tricks; Hieronymus Bosch painted a version around 1500.
